steps.say: You built a React + Node.js app, and it works perfectly on your computer.
A teammate clones the project, but their Node.js version and dependencies differ — errors appear.
Moving to production hits the same problem: a different configuration behaves differently.
A container packages the app with its dependencies in an isolated environment, so it runs the same everywhere.
Docker is an open-source platform to build, package, distribute and run applications in containers.
A container holds the application and the dependencies required to run it.
Docker also provides tools to manage images, containers, networks and storage.
Package once, then use the same environment in development, testing and production.
Virtual machines run separate guest operating systems on top of the hardware through a hypervisor.
Containers isolate applications and their dependencies while sharing the host operating system’s kernel.
Containers generally need fewer resources and start faster than virtual machines.

pl.text: Heavier · each VM runs its own OS

steps.say: Choose by need: separate operating systems → VMs; portable apps and efficient resources → containers.
Download Docker Desktop from the official website for your operating system.
Install it and start Docker Desktop.
Docker Desktop is running, so the terminal can talk to Docker.
Verify the installation: the version and the daemon information are displayed.
docker run hello-world downloads the test image if needed, creates a container and prints a confirmation.
The Docker Client is where you type commands.
It talks to the Docker Daemon (dockerd) on the Docker Host, which manages images, containers, networks and volumes.
A registry stores and distributes images. Docker Hub is a commonly used one.
docker run nginx: the Daemon checks locally, pulls the image from the registry if missing, then creates the container.
A Docker image is a read-only template used to create containers.
It contains the application code, runtime, libraries and dependencies — built as layers.
Docker reuses existing layers, so another image built on the same base avoids repeating that work.
For example, start from an existing Node.js image instead of installing Node.js every time.

tip.text: FROM node:20  → no manual Node.js install

steps.say: A container is an instance created from an image. The image is the template.
The container is where the application actually runs — with its own writable layer.
Many containers can be created from the same image, and each one operates independently.
Containers can be stopped…
…restarted or removed — without modifying the original image.
docker pull downloads the Nginx image from the registry.
docker images lists the images available locally.
docker run creates and starts a container. -d runs it in the background; -p maps host port 8080 to container port 80.
Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser to reach the Nginx welcome page.
docker ps shows running containers.
docker stop halts the container; docker ps -a still lists it.
docker start brings it back.
docker logs displays the container’s output, so you can monitor the application.
A stopped container can be removed with docker rm.

subtopics.title: Why Do We Need a Dockerfile?

steps.say: A Node.js app needs a runtime version, dependencies and configuration. Preparing this by hand is repetitive.

man.title: Manual setup — repeated on every server

steps.say: A Dockerfile captures the environment and build instructions in one text file…
…Docker builds an image from it, and that image can be reused across environments.
FROM picks the base image; WORKDIR sets the working directory inside the image.

d2.sub: Sets the working directory inside the image

steps.say: COPY brings application files into the image; RUN executes commands while the image is built.

d1.sub: Copies application files into the image

steps.say: EXPOSE documents the port the app uses; ENV defines environment variables.

d1.sub: Documents the port used by the application

steps.say: CMD sets the default command that runs when a container starts.

d1.sub: Specifies the default command executed when a container starts

subtopics.title: Create a Dockerfile for a Node.js App

steps.say: Start with the project: server.js, package.json, package-lock.json — and a new file named Dockerfile.
Use Node.js as the base image and create a working directory.
Copy the package files first, then install dependencies.
Copy the remaining application files and document the port.
The final instruction defines the command used to start the application.

subtopics.title: Build and Run a Custom Image

steps.say: Open the terminal in the project directory — the folder with the Dockerfile.
docker build creates the image. -t names it; the dot is the build context (the current directory).
docker run starts a container from the new image and maps port 3000.
If the app listens on port 3000, it is reachable at http://localhost:3000.
Each Dockerfile instruction produces an image layer.
Change server.js: layers above the change are reused from cache; only the layers after it are rebuilt.
That is why package files and dependencies come before frequently changing source files.

note.text: npm install runs again on every code change

steps.say: Tags identify image versions, such as v1 and v2.

subtopics.title: Why Do We Need Persistent Storage?

steps.say: Containers are replaceable. A database container stores user records in its writable layer.
Remove the container and the data stored only in its writable layer is lost.
Volumes and bind mounts store data outside the writable layer.
Now the container can be removed — the data stays.
A new container attaches to the same volume and finds the records.
A volume is storage managed by Docker, independent of any container’s lifecycle.
List the available volumes.
Mount it in a MySQL container: mydata appears at /var/lib/mysql, where MySQL keeps its files.
term: $ docker run -d --name my-database -v mydata:/var/lib/mysql -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=example mysql:8

steps.say: Remove the container: the volume remains, unless the volume itself is deleted.
A bind mount connects a directory on the host machine to a location inside a container.
Mount the current directory at /app inside a Node.js container.
Edit a file on the host and the container sees the change.
That is especially useful during development.

dev.text: Edit locally · run inside the container

steps.say: An app often has a frontend, a backend and a database in separate containers. They need a way to talk.
Docker Networking provides that connectivity.
Common network drivers: Bridge, Host, None and Overlay.
Bridge connects containers on the same Docker host.
Create a custom bridge network.
Run the first container on the network.
Run a second container on the same network.
On the same user-defined bridge network, containers communicate using their container names.
No ports are published, so these services are not exposed directly to the outside world.

subtopics.title: Why Do We Need Docker Compose?

steps.say: A typical web app has a frontend, a backend and a database, each in its own container.
Managing them one by one takes many commands and separate configurations.
Compose defines all services in one YAML file…
…and manages them together with a single command.
Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications from a file, commonly named compose.yaml.
The file describes services, ports, environment variables, networks and volumes.
Instead of starting every container separately, a single command starts the entire application.
The web service runs Nginx and publishes port 8080.
The db service runs MySQL with a root password from an environment variable.
The named volume db-data keeps database files outside the container’s writable layer.
Compose also creates a default network, so the services can reach each other.
docker compose up -d starts all services in the background.
docker compose ps lists the running services.
docker compose logs shows the application logs.
docker compose down removes the containers and the network. Named volumes are kept by default.
depends_on controls start order: the backend waits for the database service.
Environment variables supply configuration, such as the database host and port.
Both services share a network, so the database is reachable using its service name db as the hostname.

modules.title: Docker Hub, Image Distribution & Best Practices

subtopics.title: Why Do We Need Docker Hub?

steps.say: You built a Docker image on your computer.
Teammates and servers need it too. Rebuilding on every machine is unnecessary work.
A container registry stores images centrally. Docker Hub is a popular one.
A repository is a collection of related images. Tags identify versions or variants.
Push uploads an image to the registry; pull downloads it.
Public repositories allow open access; private repositories restrict it to authorized users.

subtopics.title: Upload an Image to Docker Hub

steps.say: Create an account on hub.docker.com and a repository named my-node-app.
Authenticate with Docker Hub.
Tag the image with your username — the same image gets a registry-ready name and version.
Push it. The image is now in the registry for users with the required permissions.

subtopics.title: Download and Run a Published Image

steps.say: The image is published on Docker Hub.
docker pull downloads the published image.
docker run creates a container from it.
The same packaged application runs on another machine, with no manual environment setup.
Use trusted base images with a specific version, not whatever “latest” currently means.

pl.text: Use trusted, appropriately versioned base images

steps.say: Keep credentials out of Dockerfiles, and run as a non-root user where possible.

p2.text: No credentials in Dockerfiles · non-root users

steps.say: .dockerignore keeps unneeded files — dependencies, Git history, logs, env files — out of the build context.
Multi-stage builds separate the build environment from the runtime environment, reducing the final image size.

sm.text: Smaller final image · fewer unnecessary dependencies

modules.title: Docker in a Real DevOps Workflow

subtopics.title: Connect Docker to the DevOps Lifecycle

steps.say: Git manages the source code and GitHub supports collaboration.
Automation tests the application…
…builds a Docker image, publishes it to a registry and deploys it.
Docker packages the app and its dependencies so it runs consistently in every environment.
After changing the code, stage, commit and push it.
Package the app using its Dockerfile.
Run a container to confirm the app works in the environment the Dockerfile defines.

ok.text: App runs in the Dockerfile’s environment

steps.say: GitHub Actions can run whenever code is pushed or a pull request is created.

n6.text: Push the image to Docker Hub

steps.say: It checks out the code, installs dependencies and runs the automated tests.
Then it builds the Docker image.
Registry credentials come from GitHub Actions secrets — never hard-coded in workflow files.

wn.text: No hard-coded credentials in workflow files

steps.say: Finally the image is pushed to Docker Hub.
Once the image is published, a deployment server can retrieve it from Docker Hub.
Download the image…
…and run it. The application now runs inside a container on the server.
Production may also need persistent storage, environment variables, monitoring, health checks and extra security.
A developer adds a feature to the task management app and pushes it to GitHub.
GitHub Actions automatically runs the tests and builds a Docker image.
The changes pass the required checks.
The image is published to Docker Hub.
The deployment server pulls the image and starts a container with the required configuration.
The updated application becomes available to users.

sm.text: Git · GitHub · Docker · Docker Hub · CI/CD = one delivery process
